content:
Quick answer: These smoothie recipes are food ideas, not treatments for arthritis or a promise of less joint pain. Keep taking prescribed medicines and follow your care plan. NHS advice is to limit fruit or vegetable juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml a day, with meals.

Five smoothie ideas using everyday ingredients

The ingredient lists below make larger batches, not a recommended single serving. Blend until smooth and divide into small portions. Adjust flavour or thickness to taste, and check ingredients for allergies or dietary restrictions. There is no need to add supplements.

1. Beetroot and berry smoothie

  • 1 small cooked beetroot (peeled, chopped)
  • 1 cup frozen mixed berries
  • 1 banana
  • 1-inch fresh ginger, grated
  • 1 cup unsweetened almond milk
  • 1 tbsp ground flaxseed

Blend the ingredients and divide into small portions. These ingredients are included for food and flavour, not a measured therapeutic effect.

2. Mango and turmeric smoothie

  • 1 frozen banana
  • 1 cup mango chunks
  • 1 tsp turmeric powder
  • Pinch of black pepper, optional for flavour
  • Water or extra unsweetened oat milk to adjust thickness
  • 1 cup unsweetened oat milk

Blend the ingredients and divide into small portions. These ingredients are included for food and flavour, not a measured therapeutic effect.

3. Green apple and spinach smoothie

  • 2 handfuls spinach
  • 1 green apple
  • 1/2 avocado
  • Juice of 1 lemon
  • 1-inch fresh ginger
  • 1 cup water
  • 1 tbsp chia seeds

Blend the ingredients and divide into small portions. These ingredients are included for food and flavour, not a measured therapeutic effect.

4. Cherry and yoghurt smoothie

  • 1 cup frozen tart cherries
  • 1 banana
  • 1 cup Greek yoghurt
  • No added honey is needed; adjust sweetness with the fruit
  • 1/2 cup pomegranate juice

Blend the ingredients and divide into small portions. These ingredients are included for food and flavour, not a measured therapeutic effect.

5. Blueberry, walnut and yoghurt smoothie

  • 1 cup frozen blueberries
  • 2 tbsp walnuts
  • 1 tbsp hemp seeds
  • 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
  • 1 cup plain yoghurt made with pasteurised milk
  • 1 tsp cinnamon

Blend the ingredients and divide into small portions. These ingredients are included for food and flavour, not a measured therapeutic effect.

Portion size and teeth

NHS advice is to limit fruit juice, vegetable juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml a day. Crushing fruit releases sugars that can damage teeth. Have smoothies with a meal rather than sipping them between meals. A larger batch should not be treated as a daily serving.

Are these anti-inflammatory treatments?

No. Nutrients and plant compounds are studied in different settings, but that does not establish that these particular recipes reduce arthritis symptoms. A smoothie cannot replace your medicines, exercise advice or other care. Use it as one food choice within a varied diet, not as a daily treatment you have to follow.

NICE NG100, recommendation 1.8.8 says there is no strong evidence that experimenting with diet benefits rheumatoid arthritis, although a Mediterranean-style pattern can be encouraged. This does not amount to a recommendation for any smoothie or ingredient as treatment. NICE does not assess these recipes individually.

Food preparation and storage

Wash your hands, clean the blender and wash fresh fruit and vegetables before preparing them. Use pasteurised milk or yoghurt. Check frozen-product labels: follow preparation and cooking instructions rather than assuming every frozen ingredient is ready to blend raw. If using frozen vegetables, cook them first when the packet says to do so, even for a cold smoothie.

Keep perishable ingredients chilled, follow their use-by dates and storage instructions, and do not leave a large batch sitting at room temperature. Make a smaller batch or share it rather than treating the recipe as one serving.

Medicines, allergies and individual needs

These recipes include ingredients such as nuts, milk or dairy alternatives, seeds, ginger and turmeric. Check allergies, product labels and your own dietary advice. If you have been given a specific diet or fluid restriction, ask your clinician or dietitian how the recipes fit. If you have been told you are neutropenic or need specific food-safety precautions, ask your own team about homemade smoothies and probiotic products such as kefir; advice for these higher-risk groups is not a blanket restriction for everyone taking arthritis medicine.

If you take warfarin, keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than suddenly adding large spinach smoothies or cutting vegetables out. Cambridge University Hospitals NHS advice says not to drink pomegranate juice with warfarin, so recipe 4 is not suitable as written: ask your pharmacist about an alternative.

Concentrated supplements are different from culinary ingredients; check any supplement with a pharmacist before combining it with medicines.

Questions people ask

Do I need black pepper with turmeric?

Not for this recipe. Add it only if you like the flavour. This is not an attempt to reproduce a curcumin supplement trial, and greater supplement absorption is not automatically safer.

Should I replace meals with smoothies?

These recipes are not designed as complete meal replacements or personalised nutrition plans. If eating or maintaining weight is difficult, ask your GP or dietitian for advice.

See the arthritis diet guide and ginger and turmeric evidence and safety guide for context. General information only, not personal medical advice.
